newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE - New Zealand power market fails small consumers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New Zealand power market fails small consumers.

text.p: Six months into operation, the benefits of New Zealand's new wholesale electricity market are not feeding through to small consumers.
Most of the market's teething problems, such as price spikes and computer system glitches, have been ironed out and attention has switched to what many say are deeper, underlying flaws.
The market, which kicked into operation on October 1, 1996, aims to determine the price of electricity based on supply and demand, as opposed to the cost-based method of the past.

New Zealand has for several years been working to neutralise the power of the natural monopolies that pervaded its electricity industry. If it pulls it off, some believe it could become a world leader in electricity reforms.
David Russell, chief executive of the Consumers Institute, supported the concept of a competitive market, but said it was driven by a dream.
"Insufficient recognition was given to the reality of how that dream was going to be realised," he said.

"The whole reason, the rationale, for the establishment of the market was to deliver a better service to the consumers of New Zealand in terms of quality and in terms of price. That certainly has not occurred for the small user."
GIVE CONSUMERS A CHOICE
Lincoln Gould, chief executive of the Electricity Market Company (EMCO), which operates the new market, said the first six months of operation were encouraging.
"The electricity system is now being operated with a transparency that will allow further efficiencies and cost reductions," he said.
However, many market participants trying to manage their risk were struggling with the sheer amount of information on offer and it was not being used as widely as EMCO hoped.

Gould agreed the delivery of the open market to small consumers was proving problematic. Consumers had no incentive to manage their electricity consumption because distribution companies were not providing the price information necessary for them to make a choice, he said.
Greg Sise, managing director of industry consultants Energy Link, questioned whether smaller electricity users would utilise that information.
He argued that the vast majority were not interested in monitoring price signals on a daily basis and leaping from their armchairs to switch off the lights if prices rose too far.

"It comes back really to the equipment manufacturers and the power companies thinking of innovative ways of managing risk, and providing some very simple signals, based on that risk management, to the consumer," Sise said.
He suggested smart appliances that could switch off when electricity prices rose too high.
Russell said new metering technology may be available later this year which would allow consumers to dial up their preferred electricity supplier, based on the range of prices on offer.

However, regional distribution companies would maintain a monopoly over the delivery of that energy, and the profit margins would probably be too small to entice many power companies to chase business outside their own region.
LACKS TRANSPARENCY, COMPETITION
Russell said it was a mistake, when the electricity market reforms began, to allow local retail power companies to retain their power distribution businesses, known as 'line'.
"If you really wanted to promote transparency and competition, you would have to split off completely the line business from the energy business," he said.
Another mistake was to deregulate "from the bottom up".

Geographical boundaries over supply to small electricity consumers were the first to go, giving new suppliers the ability to move in and compete. However, new entrants were not drawn to compete for the less lucrative business of smaller users.
"In a gung-ho way, New Zealand went in and deregulated from the bottom up, and it didn't really provide residual protection for consumers.

"It was said the information disclosure regulations were going to provide the protection. It's beautiful in theory, but as an individual householder even if I had the interest I wouldn't have the time to wade through all that information to make an informed decision. And then I couldn't swap companies anyway, so the whole thing becomes a farce."

Russell said the state of Victoria in Australia, which has been developing a wholesale electricity market over the last three years, seemed to be learning from New Zealand's mistakes and moving more slowly.
"Victoria is approaching the development of its market in a more pragmatic way that offers better interim protection for consumers."
ELECTRICITY FUTURES SHINE

Analysts said that while the wholesale electricity market had put in a mixed performance the electricity futures launched by the New Zealand Futures and Options Exchange (NZFOE) in November had done surprisingly well.
The contracts are the first cash-settled electricity futures in the world.

Last week Greg Boland, the NZFOE's manager of business development, said that in response to demand, the exchange planned to extend the range of one-month contracts on offer to 12 months out, from a maxiumum of six at present.
"That came quite quickly -- they're obviously feeling quite confident," said Energy Link's Sise.
"Certainly from the purchasers' point of view the exchange-traded contracts are very attractive. They're easy, they're immediate, and they're totally standardised."
Boland said the market was not drawing speculators at present, but he was confident this would change.
"Once the market is more active I expect it will attract people from outside the electricity industry, which is a real benefit as current hedge mechanisms just spread risk through the industry."
